newsitem.title: INDIA: India ready for early peace talks with Pakistan.
newsitem.headline: India ready for early peace talks with Pakistan.

text.p: India is committed to improving relations with Pakistan and hopes for the early resumption of bilateral peace talks, President Shankar Dayal Sharma said on Thursday.

"With Pakistan, we are committed to ending confrontation and establishing a harmonious relationship and durable peace, as provided for in the Shimla Agreement," Sharma said in a speech to parliament at the start of its budget session.
India and Pakistan pledged in their 1972 Shimla Agreement to resolve differences through peaceful means in bilateral negotiations.

"We believe that fostering people-to-people contacts and promoting trade and economic links will contribute to this process," Sharma said in his speech, which had earlier been cleared by Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's cabinet.
Foreign Minister Inder Kumar Gujral has pushed for easing restrictions on travel between the two countries and strengthening trade ties.
But Pakistan has balked at extending most favoured trade (MFN) status to India, saying longstanding bilateral political strains must first be relieved.
In extending MFN, a country undertakes to give another nation the maximum tariff concessions which it already grants to other trading partners.
"We are ready for dialogue with the new government of Pakistan and hope for an early resumption of talks," the Indian president said.

On Tuesday, Deve Gowda said in a letter to Pakistan's new prime minister, Nawaz Sharif, that India wanted to resume peace talks which broke down in early 1994, and was willing to discuss a wide range of issues including disputed Kashmir.

India and Pakistan have fought three wars since independence in 1947, two of them sparked by tension over Kashmir. India, which controls two thirds of the Himalayan region, says Kashmir is an integral part of its territory.
Successive Pakistani governments have insisted that the people of mainly Moslem Kashmir must be allowed to vote on whether to join Islamic Pakistan or Hindu-majority India.
Sharif's electoral victory has raised hopes that the two countries could soon resume talks.
Last week Deve Gowda said he favoured fresh talks, but would never relinquish the area of Kashmir which is in India's Jammu and Kashmir state.
Pakistan said on Friday that Deve Gowda's offer of talks was pointless unless the subject of Kashmir was on the table.
